newsitem.title: INDIA: India says not isolated in import dispute.
newsitem.headline: India says not isolated in import dispute.

text.p: India denied on Friday that its trading partners had isolated it in a dispute over import restrictions, and said they appeared eager to reach a negotiated settlement with New Delhi.

Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah said a group of developed nations, including the United States, had brought a case against India in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) after talks over India's import curbs ended without agreement last month.

The European Union, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Switzerland joined Washington in arguing that India's decades-old import restrictions violated world trade agreements, and referred the row to the WTO's dispute settlement process.
"India has accepted the requests for consultations," Ramaiah said in a written reply to a question by a deputy in the lower house.
"There are indications that the complainants would like to work towards a mutually acceptable solution. India's approach to these consultations would also be similar."

The trade restrictions, which affect some 2,700 items ranging from consumer goods to farm products, have been in force since the 1950s, but were accepted by other countries because of India's earlier balance of payments problems.
But with steady growth in the country's foreign exchange reserves, which reached $29.45 billion last month, other WTO members have insisted that New Delhi drop the curbs.
India initially proposed dismantling the restrictions over nine years, but, under pressure, offered to do so in six years, Ramaiah said last month.

The United States was reportedly pressing for a three-year phase-out of the curbs, while the EU and other WTO members indicated five years would be acceptable if limits on most big-ticket items were removed early on.
After two rounds of talks in June and July ended without an agreement, India's trading partners referred the matter to the WTO's dispute settlement procedure.

Ramaiah referred to a recent Indian newspaper article that said New Delhi risked isolation in the world trade arena by refusing to propose an internationally acceptable time frame for scrapping the barriers, mostly import quotas.
But he said some members of the WTO's Committee on Balance of Payments Restrictions found India's proposal "workable".
"Therefore, it may not be correct to state that India was isolated during the deliberations of this committee," Ramaiah said.
